title: Teaching Children the Fruit of Longsuffering
author: Humanitas Institute
summary: This essay argues that today's unusually attentive, anxious generation of parents often confuses two different acts of love: protecting a child from cruelty, which is right, and protecting a child from difficulty, which quietly deforms the soul it means to nurture. Drawing on the Greek concept of schole (leisure understood as unhurried, purposeful engagement, not ease), Aristotle's account of virtue as habituated through repeated hard practice, and C.S. Lewis's warning against an education that trains intellect while never testing the affections, the piece builds a theological and philosophical case for productive struggle as formation rather than punishment. Homework serves as the central case study, with the author distinguishing three different roots of a child's evening struggle — defiance, apathy, and genuine exhaustion — that each call for a different parental response, while insisting the parent's real job is neither to rescue the child from difficulty nor to blame the child for it. The essay extends this logic across the full architecture of a classical education (memory work, difficult texts, minimal screens) and closes on Augustine's definition of virtue as rightly ordered love, arguing that classical rigor is itself a form of mercy aimed at producing durable endurance rather than gritted-teeth suffering.
points: The essay draws a sharp distinction between schole (unhurried, purposeful engagement worth doing for its own sake) and mere ease, arguing that removing all effort and discomfort from childhood 'asks nothing of the soul and therefore forms nothing in it.'

Citing Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, the author argues virtue does not arise by nature but by habituation — by doing the hard, repeated thing until it becomes who a person is — which frames sustained struggle as formation rather than an obstacle to a flourishing childhood.

The piece offers a practical diagnostic for parents facing homework struggle: distinguish defiance (needs a firm boundary without lecturing), apathy (needs a reminder of the work's value paired with an immovable standard), and genuine exhaustion (needs tender accommodation, not rigid firmness) — because treating one condition with the response suited to another 'misdirects the soul's training at every turn.'

Quoting Charlotte Mason ('the formation of habits is education, and education is the formation of habits'), the essay argues homework's real purpose is not the worksheet content but training a child to show up for a hard thing consistently, and training a parent to sit beside the difficulty rather than rescue from it or resent the assigner.

The essay extends its argument beyond homework to the full architecture of classical education — difficult texts, memory work, minimal screens — framing all of it as 'sacred toil' rather than cruelty, and closes with Augustine's definition of virtue as rightly ordered love: a parent's love for a child's present comfort becomes disordered when it is placed above the child's long-term formation.
quotes: Ease is not schole; ease asks nothing of the soul and therefore forms nothing in it.
It comes by habituation, by doing the hard, repeated thing until it becomes who we are.
As Lewis wrote in The Abolition of Man, "The task of the modern educator is not to cut down jungles, but to irrigate deserts.
The parent's actual task in that moment is neither to blame nor to rescue, but to sit inside the difficulty alongside the child.
Charlotte Mason put the underlying principle as plainly as it can be put: "the formation of habits is education, and education is the formation of habits.
None of it is cruelty, rather, it is sacred toil because a soul does not learn to bear weight by never being asked to carry any.
Rightly ordered love does not spare a child every cost. It counts the cost and pays it anyway because it loves the child's future more than it fears the child's present frustration.

Not suffering as an end, but suffering as a seed, borne now, in the safety of a classroom and a parent's watchful presence, so that it yields a harvest of endurance, humility, and hope no shortcut could ever produce.
